extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, scholars, and practitioners interested in comedy (writers, performers, critics)
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic overview of comedy: definitions, historical origins, major forms/subgenres, techniques, and theories of what produces laughter. Useful as a reference for understanding or producing comedic work across media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy — general definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy is a genre of dramatic works intended to be humorous or amusing by inducing laughter, especially in theatre, film, stand-up comedy, television, radio, books, or any other entertainment medium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets the primary evaluative criterion for a work being 'comedy': its intent and effect (to amuse / induce laughter). Applies across media; the article lists common media where comedy appears.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greek/Aristophanic comedic agon (origin and structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: The theatrical genre of Greek comedy can be described as a dramatic performance pitting two groups, ages, genders, or societies against each other in an amusing agon or conflict. A revised view characterizes the essential agon of comedy as a struggle between a relatively powerless youth and the societal conventions posing obstacles to his hopes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this model, the protagonist resorts to ruses that engender dramatic irony which provokes laughter. This historical pattern is a useful structural criterion for certain comedies (conflict-driven, ironic resolution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristotle's definition of comedy (the Ridiculous)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle defined comedy as an imitation of men worse than the average; the Ridiculous may be defined as a mistake or deformity not productive of pain or harm to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle's view implies comedic characters are 'lesser' in a way that provokes laughter without cruelty. The article also notes a pattern: comedies begin with low/base characters seeking insignificant aims and end with some accomplishment that lightens the baseness or reveals insignificance of the aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire and political satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire and political satire use comedy to portray people or social institutions as ridiculous or corrupt, thus alienating their audience from the object of their humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functionally, satire's evaluative criterion is its ability to critique social/political targets by exposing folly or corruption; it often aims for alienation from the target rather than mere amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody
rubrics_metrics.description: Parody subverts popular genres and forms, critiquing those forms without necessarily condemning them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parody's success is judged by how well it imitates the conventions of its target and then subverts them to reveal or critique those conventions; examples include satirical news formats (The Onion, The Colbert Report).

rubrics_metrics.name: Surreal / absurdist humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Surreal humour (also known as 'absurdist humour') is predicated on deliberate violations of causal reasoning, producing events and behaviours that are obviously illogical; constructions tend to involve bizarre juxtapositions, incongruity, non-sequiturs, irrational or absurd situations and expressions of nonsense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humour arises from subversion of audience expectations and unpredictability rather than logical analysis. Roots in Surrealism; examples cited include Lewis Carroll and Edward Lear. Useful criteria for evaluating absurdist pieces: degree of illogic, incongruity, and unpredictability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Screwball, black, and taboo-based comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Screwball comedy derives its humor largely from bizarre, surprising (and improbable) situations or characters; black comedy is characterized by humor that includes darker aspects of human behavior or human nature. Similarly scatological, sexual, and race humor create comedy by violating social conventions or taboos, which can often be taken as offensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating these forms, consider the balance between shock/taboo and audience reception: whether transgression serves comedic purpose or only offends. The article flags potential offensiveness as a consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy of manners
rubrics_metrics.description: A comedy of manners typically takes as its subject a particular part of society (usually upper-class society) and uses humor to parody or satirize the behavior and mannerisms of its members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effectiveness judged by the accuracy and sharpness of social observation and the wit of the parody of manners and conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Romantic comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Romantic comedy depicts burgeoning romance in humorous terms and focuses on the foibles of those who are falling in love.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative criteria include chemistry between characters, comedic treatment of foibles, and a tone that balances romance with humor (often culminating in reconciliatory/happy endings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stand-up comedy mode
rubrics_metrics.description: Stand-up comedy is a mode of comic performance in which the performer addresses the audience directly, usually speaking in their own person rather than as a dramatic character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristics to evaluate include directness, persona, timing, material (observational, anecdotal, social/political), and delivery. The article situates stand-up within clubs, festivals, and related forms (alternative comedy, impressionism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-deprecation as technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-deprecation is a technique of comedy used by many comedians who focus on their misfortunes and foibles in order to entertain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When used well it creates rapport and relatability; overuse or tone can undermine effectiveness. It's listed as one of many common comedic techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: The comic frame (rhetorical function of comedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kenneth Burke writes that the 'comic frame' in rhetoric is 'neither wholly euphemistic, nor wholly debunking—hence it provides the charitable attitude towards people that is required for purposes of persuasion and co-operation, but at the same time maintains our shrewdness concerning the simplicities of 'cashing in.' The purpose of the comic frame is to satirize a given circumstance and promote change by doing so. The comic frame makes fun of situations and people, while simultaneously provoking thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative emphasis is on balance: comedy as a tool for critique that rebukes stupidity without vilifying, and that can persuade or promote change (example: The Daily Show).

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological theories of humor (incongruity, shock, superiority)
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychologists agree the predominant characteristics connected with laughter are incongruity or contrast in the object and shock or emotional seizure on the part of the subject. It has also been held that the feeling of superiority is an essential factor (Thomas Hobbes: 'sudden glory').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These theories provide evaluative lenses: measure how much a joke produces incongruity, surprise/shock, or a sense of superiority, and how those mechanisms contribute to laughter/response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre- and form-based taxonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy may be divided into multiple genres based on the source of humor, the method of delivery, and the context in which it is delivered; different forms often overlap and most comedy can fit into multiple genres (examples: farce, comedy of manners, burlesque, satire, slapstick, sketch, stand-up, musical comedy, improvisational comedy, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this taxonomy to classify and evaluate a piece by source/method/context; overlap means multiple criteria may apply simultaneously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance-specific techniques (wordplay, timing, minimal props)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different cultural forms emphasize specific techniques: Xiangsheng (crosstalk) emphasizes word play and allusions; Rakugo is a single seated performer narrating humorous tales using dialogue, vocal variation, and minimal props.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate effectiveness by skill in the form's characteristic techniques: wordplay complexity, vocal variation, use of minimalism, pacing, and cultural resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/ cultural grounding as evaluative context
rubrics_metrics.description: The article outlines historical developments (Ancient Greece, commedia dell'arte, music hall, vaudeville, film, radio, television) and regional traditions (Indian, Chinese, Japanese forms), implying comedy should be understood and evaluated in its historical and cultural context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider historical lineage, conventions inherited from earlier forms, and cultural specificity when judging authenticity, innovation, or appropriateness of comedic work.
